items.followUp: Calculate the formula mass of calcium carbonate (CaCO₃).

rubric.why: Correct relative atomic masses are needed to calculate the formula mass.
rubric.description: Uses the correct relative atomic masses: K = 39, S = 32 and O = 16.
rubric.how: Award for listing the correct values for the elements in K₂SO₄.

rubric.why: The formula has two potassium atoms, one sulphur atom and four oxygen atoms.
rubric.description: Sets up the calculation using the correct number of each atom.
rubric.how: Award for correctly multiplying each relative atomic mass by its subscript and adding the terms.

rubric.why: This is the calculated formula mass of K₂SO₄.
rubric.description: Gives the formula mass as 174 amu.
rubric.how: Award for the correct final value with an appropriate unit.

modelAnswer: Relative atomic masses: K = 39, S = 32, O = 16.
Formula mass of K₂SO₄ = (2 × 39) + 32 + (4 × 16).

items.followUp: Describe how ionic compounds are formed and give two of their general properties.

rubric.why: Covalent bonding forms when atoms share electrons.
rubric.description: Explains that covalent compounds form by sharing electron pairs between atoms.
rubric.how: Award for stating that atoms share electrons or electron pairs to form covalent bonds.

rubric.why: Covalent compounds generally have weak forces between their molecules.
rubric.description: Gives their generally low melting and boiling points.
rubric.how: Award for identifying both melting point and boiling point as generally low.

rubric.why: Covalent compounds generally lack mobile charged particles.
rubric.description: States that covalent compounds generally do not conduct electricity.
rubric.how: Award for stating poor or no electrical conductivity.

rubric.why: Many covalent substances have low melting and boiling points.
rubric.description: States that they are often gases, liquids or soft solids.
rubric.how: Award for naming these common physical states.

rubric.why: This is a common solubility property of covalent compounds.
rubric.description: States that they are generally insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents.
rubric.how: Award for correctly stating both parts of the solubility comparison.

modelAnswer: Covalent compounds are formed when atoms, usually non-metal atoms, share one or more pairs of electrons to complete their outer shells.
They generally have low melting and boiling points.
They generally do not conduct electricity.
They are often gases, liquids or soft solids.
They are generally insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents.

items.followUp: Define electronegativity and describe its trend across a period and down a group.

rubric.why: Electropositive character is the tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions.
rubric.description: Defines electropositive character.
rubric.how: Award for connecting the tendency to lose electrons with formation of positive ions.

rubric.why: Effective nuclear attraction generally increases across a period, making electron loss less likely.
rubric.description: States that electropositive character decreases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award for the correct direction of the periodic trend.

rubric.why: The outer electrons are farther from the nucleus down a group and are lost more readily.
rubric.description: States that electropositive character increases down a group.
rubric.how: Award for the correct direction of the group trend.

modelAnswer: Electropositive character is the tendency of an atom to lose electrons and form positive ions.
Across a period, electropositive character decreases from left to right.
Down a group, electropositive character increases.

items.followUp: Define gram atomic mass and give one example.

rubric.why: Gram formula mass is the mass of one mole of formula units expressed in grams.
rubric.description: Defines gram formula mass.
rubric.how: Award for stating that it is the mass in grams of one mole (Avogadro's number) of formula units.

rubric.why: NaCl has a formula mass of 58.5 amu, so its gram formula mass is 58.5 g.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example with its gram formula mass.
rubric.how: Award for a correct substance and corresponding gram formula mass.

modelAnswer: Gram formula mass is the mass, in grams, of one mole (Avogadro’s number) of formula units of a substance.
For example, the formula mass of NaCl is 58.5 amu, so its gram formula mass is 58.5 g.

items.followUp: Give two characteristics of canal rays.

rubric.why: Cathode rays travel in straight lines from the cathode.
rubric.description: States that cathode rays travel in straight lines.
rubric.how: Award for a correct statement about their straight-line path.

rubric.why: Cathode rays consist of negatively charged particles and are deflected by fields.
rubric.description: Gives another correct characteristic, such as their negative charge or deflection by an electric or magnetic field.
rubric.how: Award for any one additional correct characteristic.

modelAnswer: Cathode rays travel in straight lines from the cathode.
They consist of negatively charged particles and are deflected by electric and magnetic fields.

items.followUp: How many protons and neutrons are present in the atom ²³₁₁Na?

rubric.why: The atomic number gives the number of protons in an atom.
rubric.description: Gives the number of protons as 17.
rubric.how: Award for the correct proton count.

rubric.why: Neutrons equal the mass number minus the atomic number.
rubric.description: Calculates and gives the number of neutrons as 18.
rubric.how: Award for the correct neutron count.

modelAnswer: Number of protons = atomic number = 17.
Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 35 − 17 = 18.

items.followUp: Which blocks are used to divide the elements in the Periodic Table?

rubric.why: The Periodic Table is divided into four blocks according to the subshell being filled.
rubric.description: Names all four blocks: s, p, d and f.
rubric.how: Award for naming all four blocks; award partial credit for naming some of them.

modelAnswer: The elements in the Periodic Table are grouped into four blocks: s-block, p-block, d-block and f-block.

items.followUp: How does the boiling point of a liquid affect its rate of evaporation?

rubric.why: A liquid with a lower boiling point generally evaporates more readily.
rubric.description: States that a lower-boiling liquid evaporates faster.
rubric.how: Award for the correct relationship between lower boiling point and faster evaporation.

rubric.why: A liquid with a higher boiling point generally evaporates less readily under the same conditions.
rubric.description: States that a higher-boiling liquid evaporates more slowly.
rubric.how: Award for the correct reverse relationship.

modelAnswer: A liquid with a lower boiling point evaporates faster.
A liquid with a higher boiling point evaporates more slowly, under the same conditions.
